paragraphs: 1. The Edicts, Constitutions, and Letters of the Prince — that is, of the Emperor — because the whole power of the people resided in him. Like these are the proclamations of the kings of England.

2. The Decrees of the whole people of Rome (the Senate included), when they were put to the vote by the Senate. These were laws, at first, by virtue of the sovereign power residing in the people; and such of them as the emperors did not abrogate remained laws by imperial authority. For every law that binds is understood to bind by the authority of whoever has the power to repeal it. Something like these laws are the Acts of Parliament in England.

3. The Decrees of the common people (excluding the Senate), when they were put to the vote by the tribune of the people. Such of these as the emperors did not abrogate remained laws by imperial authority. Something like these were the Orders of the House of Commons in England.

4. Senatus consulta, the Orders of the Senate — because when the people of Rome grew so numerous that assembling them became inconvenient, the emperor thought it best that men consult the Senate in the people's place. These bear some resemblance to Acts of Council.
5. The Edicts of the Praetors, and in some cases of the Aediles — comparable to the Chief Justices in the courts of England.

6. Responsa Prudentum: the opinions and rulings of those lawyers to whom the emperor gave authority to interpret the law and to answer those who came to them in matters of law for advice. Judges, in delivering judgement, were bound by the emperor's constitutions to follow these rulings — they would be like the reports of decided cases, if other judges were bound by the law of England to follow them. For the judges of the common law of England are not, properly speaking, judges at all, but juris consulti — men of law whose advice the true judges, whether the Lords or twelve men of the country, are to seek on points of law.
7. Also, unwritten customs — which by their own nature imitate law — are, by the tacit consent of the emperor, true laws in themselves, provided they do not contradict the law of nature.

There is another division of laws, into natural and positive. Natural laws are those that have been laws from all eternity, and are called not only natural but also moral laws, consisting in the moral virtues — justice, equity, and all the habits of mind that promote peace and charity — of which I have already spoken in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters.

Positive laws are those that have not existed from eternity, but have been made laws by the will of those who have held sovereign power over others, and are either put in writing or otherwise made known to men as an expression of their legislator's will.

Again, of positive laws, some are human and some divine; and of human positive laws, some are distributive and some penal. Distributive laws are those that determine the rights of subjects, declaring to every man what it is by which he acquires and holds property in lands or goods, and a right or liberty of action — these speak to all subjects alike. Penal laws are those that declare what penalty shall be inflicted on those who break the law, and these speak to the ministers and officers appointed to carry out that execution. For although every man ought to be informed beforehand of the punishments set for his own transgression, the command itself is not addressed to the offender (who cannot be expected to punish himself faithfully), but to the public ministers charged with seeing the penalty carried out. These penal laws are for the most part written together with the distributive laws, and are sometimes called judgements — for all laws are general judgements, or sentences, of the legislator, just as every particular judgement is a law to the man whose case is judged.

Divine positive laws (for the natural laws, being eternal and universal, are all divine already) are those which, being commandments of God — not from all eternity, nor addressed to all men universally, but only to a certain people or to certain persons — are declared to be such by those whom God has authorised to declare them. But how can this authority of a man to declare what these positive laws of God are be known? God may command a man, by some supernatural means, to deliver laws to other men. But since it belongs to the very essence of law that the man who is to be obliged be assured of the authority of the one declaring it — and since we have no natural way of recognising that authority as coming from God — how can a man, without a revelation of his own, be assured of the revelation received by the one who declares it? And how can he be bound to obey it? As to the first question — how a man can be assured of another's revelation without a revelation particular to himself — the answer is plainly that he cannot. For although a man may be led to believe in such a revelation by the miracles he sees the other perform, or by the extraordinary holiness of his life, or by the extraordinary wisdom or extraordinary success of his actions (all of which are marks of God's special favour), none of these amount to assured evidence of a special revelation. Miracles are marvellous works, but what is marvellous to one man may not be so to another. Holiness can be feigned, and the visible good fortune of this world is, more often than not, the work of God through natural and ordinary causes. And so no man can know with certainty, by natural reason alone, that another has received a supernatural revelation of God's will — he can only believe it, more or less firmly, depending on how strong the signs of it appear to him.

But as to the second question — how he can be bound to obey it — that is not so hard. For if the law declared is not contrary to the law of nature (which is undoubtedly God's law), and he agrees to obey it, then he is bound by his own act — bound, I say, to obey it, but not bound to believe it. For men's beliefs and inward thoughts are not subject to command, but only to the working of God, whether ordinary or extraordinary. Faith in a supernatural law is not a fulfilling of that law, but merely an assenting to it — not a duty we render to God, but a gift God freely gives to whomever he pleases; just as unbelief is not the breaking of any of his laws, but a rejection of all of them except the natural ones. But what I am saying here will become still clearer through examples and testimonies on this point from Holy Scripture. The covenant God made with Abraham, in a supernatural manner, was this (Gen. 17:10): 'This is the covenant which you shall keep between me and you and your descendants after you.' Abraham's descendants had received no such revelation, and indeed did not yet exist; yet they were made party to the covenant, bound to obey whatever Abraham should declare to them as God's law — which they could only be bound to do by virtue of the obedience they already owed their parents, who (provided they were subject to no other earthly power, as was the case with Abraham) held sovereign power over their children and servants. Again, where God says to Abraham, 'In you shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, for I know that you will command your children and your household after you to keep the way of the Lord, and to observe righteousness and judgement,' it is plain that the obedience of his household, who had received no revelation of their own, rested on their prior obligation to obey their sovereign. At Mount Sinai, Moses alone went up to God; the people were forbidden to approach on pain of death; yet they were bound to obey everything Moses declared to them as God's law. On what ground, if not this submission of their own: 'Speak to us yourself, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die'? These two passages make it sufficiently clear that in a commonwealth, a subject who has no certain and assured revelation of his own concerning God's will is bound to accept as such the command of the commonwealth. For if men were free to take their own dreams and fancies — or the dreams and fancies of private individuals — as God's commandments, scarcely two men would agree about what God had commanded, and yet each would feel entitled, on that basis, to despise the commandments of the commonwealth. I conclude, therefore, that in everything not contrary to the moral law (that is, to the law of nature), all subjects are bound to obey as divine law whatever is declared to be such by the laws of the commonwealth. This is also plain to anyone's reason: for whatever is not against the law of nature may be made law in the name of those who hold sovereign power, and there is no reason why men should be any less obliged by it when it is put forward in the name of God. Besides, there is nowhere in the world where men are permitted to claim other commandments of God than those the commonwealth declares to be such. Christian states punish those who fall away from the Christian religion, and every other state punishes those who set up a religion it has forbidden. For in whatever the commonwealth has not regulated, it is equity — which is the law of nature, and therefore an eternal law of God — that every man should equally enjoy his liberty.

There is also another distinction of laws, into fundamental and not fundamental; but I have never seen, in any author, what a fundamental law actually means. Nevertheless, one may quite reasonably draw the distinction in this way.

A fundamental law, in any commonwealth, is one which, if removed, causes the commonwealth to fail and be utterly dissolved — like a building whose foundation has been destroyed. A fundamental law is therefore one by which subjects are bound to uphold whatever power has been given to the sovereign, whether a monarch or a sovereign assembly, without which the commonwealth cannot stand — such as the power of war and peace, of judicature, of the election of officers, and of doing whatever he judges necessary for the public good. A law is not fundamental if its repeal does not carry with it the dissolution of the commonwealth — such as the laws concerning disputes between one subject and another. So much, then, for the division of laws.

I find the words Lex Civilis and Jus Civile — that is, civil law and civil right — used interchangeably for the same thing, even by the most learned authors; though they should not be. For right is liberty — namely, that liberty which the civil law leaves us — but civil law is an obligation, and takes from us the liberty that the law of nature gave us. Nature gave every man a right to secure himself by his own strength, and to strike first against a neighbour he suspected; but civil law removes that liberty in every case where it is safe to wait instead for the protection of the law. So much, then, are Lex and Jus as different from one another as obligation is from liberty.

Likewise, laws and charters are commonly taken for the same thing. Yet charters are gifts from the sovereign, and are not laws but exemptions from law. The formula of a law is jubeo, injungo — 'I command,' 'I enjoin.' The formula of a charter is dedi, concessi — 'I have given,' 'I have granted.' But what is given or granted to a man is not forced upon him by a law. A law can be made to bind all the subjects of a commonwealth; a liberty, or charter, belongs only to one man, or to some one part of the people. For to say that all the people of a commonwealth have liberty in some case whatsoever is to say that, in that case, no law has been made — or else, having been made, has now been abrogated.
